ethiopia.content: MFAEthiopia BlogThe Official Blog of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of EthiopiaA Week in the Horn Skip to content MFAEthiopia Blog Home A Week in the Horn Diplomats’ Note Diaspora, Business & Economy Subscribe Log in A Week in the Horn Friday, 6 November 2026 · A Week in the Horn Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Leads Ethiopian Delegation to the 3rd Russia–Africa Summit Ethiopia Commemorates 40th Anniversary of the Right to Development with UN and AU Officials Ethiopia Takes Part in AU-EU Senior Officials’ Meeting Held in Addis Ababa NEWS IN BRIEF Ethiopia A high-level Ethiopian delegation led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed successfully concluded its participation in the Third Russia–Africa Summit, held in Moscow, Russia, on October 28–29, 2026. The Summit provided an important platform for advancing Ethiopia–Russia relations, strengthening Africa–Russia cooperation, and exploring new avenues of partnership in strategic sectors. (See article) Minister of Foreign Affairs Gedion Timothewos held discussions with China’s Special Envoy for African Affairs, Liu Xianfa, on Wednesday (November 4), exchanging views on peace and security in Africa. Minister Gedion briefed the Special Envoy on the current peace and security situation in the Horn of Africa, while Liu reaffirmed China’s commitment to playing a constructive role in promoting peace and security across the continent. FM Gedion held talks with Chinese Ambassador to Ethiopia Chen Hai on Tuesday (November 3), discussing ways to deepen the two countries’ All-Weather Strategic Partnership, particularly in trade, investment and capacity building. Ambassador Chen Hai reaffirmed China’s support for Ethiopia’s development plans. State Minister Ambassador Hadera Abera met with a delegation of the European Union Political and Security Committee (PSC), led by its Chair, Ambassador Lene Vensild, on Thursday (November 5). The discussion focused on current developments in Ethiopia, the Government’s reform efforts, regional peace and security, and Ethiopia-EU relations. State Minister Ambassador Berhanu Tsegaye received His Majesty King Letsie III of the Kingdom of Lesotho to Addis Ababa on Monday (November 2) at Bole International Airport, for his working visit to Ethiopia. Ethiopia participated in the 9th Assembly of the International Solar Alliance in New Delhi, represented by Ambassador Nebiyu Tedla, who reaffirmed the country’s commitment to renewable energy and highlighted the importance of cooperation, investment and affordable clean technologies in advancing an inclusive energy transition. Addis Ababa was recognized with the 2026 Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities on Saturday (October 31), highlighting the city’s progress in sustainable urban development and its ongoing transformation. Djibouti President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh of Djibouti received Somalia’s Speaker of the House of the People, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur, on Monday (November 2), discussing ways to strengthen bilateral ties and strategic cooperation between the two countries. Africa and the African Union Africa’s Commemoration of the 40th Anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development at the African Union Headquarters, running from November 4-6. Convening under the urgent theme “From Resilience to Sustainable Prosperity,” the high-level opening session featured addresses from Ambassador Hadera Abera, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Awa Dabo, United Nations Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, and Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security. (See article) Senior officials from the African Union, the European Commission and EU Member States convened at the AU Headquarters in Addis Ababa on Wednesday (November 4) for the AU-EU Senior Officials’ Meeting, advancing the outcomes of the 7th AU-EU Summit held in Luanda in November 2025. The meeting focused on strengthening cooperation in peace and security, multilateralism, trade, economic development, climate action, food security, and digital and AI governance, with a view to translating the Joint Vision for 2030 into concrete actions. (See article) The African Union Commission and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies convened a high-level event on Tuesday (November 3) to advance durable solutions towards zero hunger in Africa, with AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf calling for collective action and sustained commitment to resilient agrifood systems and food security across the continent. AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf received King Letsie III of Lesotho on Tuesday (November 3), on the sidelines of the AU-IFRC High-Level Event on Advancing Durable Solutions Towards Zero Hunger in Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Leads Ethiopian Delegation to the 3rd Russia–Africa Summit A high-level Ethiopian delegation led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed successfully concluded its participation in the Third Russia–Africa Summit, held in Moscow, Russia, on October 28–29, 2026. The Summit provided an important platform for advancing Ethiopia–Russia relations, strengthening Africa–Russia cooperation, and exploring new avenues of partnership in strategic sectors. The Summit concluded with the adoption of the Declaration of the Third Russia–Africa Summit and a new Action Plan for the Russia–Africa Partnership Forum, setting out priorities for cooperation and continued political dialogue between the two sides. Addressing the plenary session of the Leaders’ Summit, Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the historic foundations of Ethiopia–Russia relations, noting that the friendship between the two countries spans more than a century and is rooted in mutual respect, cooperation, and solidarity. Recalling Russia’s humanitarian contribution following the Battle of Adwa in 1896, the Prime Minister noted that the Russian Red Cross Mission provided medical assistance to wounded Ethiopian soldiers and translated a medical guide into Amharic. He described this historical contribution as a meaningful example of knowledge exchange and solidarity between the two nations. The Prime Minister went on to emphasize that Ethiopia’s development priorities are anchored in three strategic pillars: food security, energy, and knowledge. He underscored the importance of strengthening agricultural productivity through cooperation in farm machinery, agro-processing, and industrial development. On energy cooperation, he highlighted Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia towards the development of the country’s first nuclear power plant, emphasizing the importance of diversifying the national energy mix, strengthening local technical expertise, and adhering to the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). He also pointed to the broader applications of nuclear science in healthcare, including cancer treatment. Regarding knowledge and technological development, the Prime Minister highlighted Ethiopia’s ambition to advance artificial intelligence capabilities through the establishment of Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa. He invited Russian universities and research institutions to collaborate with their Ethiopian counterparts in education, research, and technological innovation. He further called for stronger economic cooperation through joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceuticals and machinery, while underscoring the importance of facilitating trade and developing efficient payment channels. On regional and international affairs, Prime Minister Abiy reiterated Ethiopia’s support for African-led mediation and negotiated solutions to conflicts on the continent. He also welcomed the adoption of the new Action Plan, stressing the need to translate summit commitments into measurable results. The Prime Minister concluded by expressing Ethiopia’s readiness to host the next Russia–Africa Summit in Addis Ababa, the seat of the African Union, underscoring the country’s commitment to strengthening the partnership between Africa and Russia. As part of his engagements in Moscow, PM Abiy attended the airshow and handover ceremony marking the delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets to the Ethiopian Defense Force. In his remarks on the occasion, the Prime Minister described the delivery as an important milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities and safeguard national sovereignty. He stated that the acquisition was made in accordance with an earlier agreement with the Russian Government and expressed appreciation to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery ahead of the agreed schedule. The Prime Minister also indicated that Ethiopia would receive four batteries of the S-400 air defense system. He underscored that strengthening the operational readiness of the Ethiopian Defense Force is an essential component of the country’s efforts to deter aggression, safeguard its security, and contribute to regional stability. Expanding beyond strategic and military cooperation into the cultural and intellectual sphere, the visit also featured the presentation of the Russian-language edition of the Prime Minister’s foundational philosophy book, Medemer. During their bilateral discussions, Prime Minister Abiy handed over a copy of the newly translated book to President Vladimir Putin. On the sidelines of the Summit, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ambassador Hadera Abera held discussions with Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation Georgy Borisenko. Their discussions focused on strengthening the Ethiopia–Russia strategic partnership, expanding economic and energy cooperation, and enhancing collaboration on regional peace, security, and multilateral issues. Another significant outcome of the Summit was the signing of three bilateral agreements between Ethiopia and Russia. The agreements comprise an Intergovernmental Agreement on Dejazmach Balcha Hospital in Addis Ababa, a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA) and Russia’s ITAR-TASS, and another Memorandum of Understanding between ENA and Russia Today (RT). The agreement concerning Dejazmach Balcha Hospital underscores the shared commitment of the two countries to strengthening healthcare cooperation, modernizing medical infrastructure, and improving the delivery of health services. The two media cooperation agreements are expected to provide a framework for enhanced information exchange, professional collaboration, and institutional partnerships between the respective media organizations. Ethiopia Commemorates 40th Anniversary of the Right to Development with UN and AU Officials Africa’s Commemoration of the 40th Anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development at the African Union Headquarters, running from November 4-6. Convening under the urgent theme “From Resilience to Sustainable Prosperity,” the high-level opening session featured addresses from Ambassador Hadera Abera, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Awa Dabo, United Nations Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, and Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security. In his address, Ambassador Hadera Abera said the gathering was not merely a moment to mark a historical milestone, but an opportunity to reflect on four decades of achievements and to deliberate on what remains to be done to fully realize the Declaration’s objectives. He recalled the vision set out in its first article: that every human person should participate in, contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development, alongside the full realization of human rights and fundamental freedoms. The Ambassador acknowledged the progress the world has made since 1986, citing reduced extreme poverty, improved access to education and health care, longer life expectancy, and advances in science and technology. He noted, however, that the global South continues to face structural impediments, including external debt burdens and technological and financing gaps, which weigh on the development prospects of States operating in a rapidly evolving global landscape. Ambassador Hadera underscored that the Declaration affirmed a truth African visionaries had long understood: development is not a privilege, nor mere charity or aid, but a fundamental human right owed to every citizen. He pointed out that Africa had anchored this principle in the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights well before 1986, demonstrating that economic and social progress must advance together with civil liberties. Today, he said, the right continues to drive the African Union’s Agenda 2063: The Africa We Want, as well as the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Describing the theme as fitting for Ethiopia’s ongoing development trajectory, the Ambassador said Ethiopia, as a founding member of both the OAU and the UN, has consistently championed the view that true self-determination is inseparable from economic independence, food security, and self-reliant national development. Human dignity, he stressed, cannot be fully realized without freedom from poverty and access to quality healthcare, clean energy, education, and meaningful economic opportunity. He said Ethiopia’s home-grown economic reform agenda has taken historic steps toward economic resilience, environmental sustainability, and food sovereignty, translating the right to development from paper into tangible outcomes for its people. Through targeted investments in cluster farming, wheat self-sufficiency programs, and irrigation, he said, Ethiopia has moved from being a net importer to an exporter of wheat. The Ambassador also pointed to the Green Legacy Initiative, under which about 56 billion tree seedlings have been planted since 2019, restoring degraded lands, fighting climate change, and building sustainable livelihoods for rural communities. By integrating fruit-bearing and livestock fodder trees into local farming systems, he said, the initiative also advances food security. He described the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Africa’s largest hydroelectric dam, planned and financed through Ethiopian capacity, as a project that is generating electricity to connect the region and embodies a model of self-reliance and shared, sustainable growth. GERD, he said, is an answer to Ethiopians’ centuries-old quest to use their resources for their own advancement, and a remarkable transformative project in Africa’s modern development history. It stands as a testament to Ethiopia’s commitment to the right to development and a practical embodiment of the Declaration’s core principle that citizens are the owners and primary beneficiaries of development’s fruits. “These initiatives prove that when a nation invests in its people, infrastructure, and natural resources, the Right to Development becomes a living reality,” he said. Speaking candidly about the realities facing the continent, Ambassador Hadera pointed to severe systemic obstacles: an unfair global financial system, crushing debt burdens, geopolitical shocks, and the disproportionate impacts of a climate crisis Africa did not create. These structural inequities, he said, strain the continent’s ability to make progress. Even so, he insisted that Africa is not a passive recipient of circumstances. Its greatest strengths lie within its own borders: a vibrant, innovative youth population, dynamic entrepreneurs, and unmatched natural wealth. He called on African countries to unlock the power of youth, empower women, and build resilient economies that leave no one behind, aligning efforts and moving forward together. At the same time, he urged continued demands for urgent reform of the global financial architecture. Africa, he said, requires equitable access to capital, fair trade systems, and robust climate adaptation financing so that its development strategies can flourish unhindered by external systemic imbalances. Concluding his remarks, Ambassador Hadera said development rights must not remain abstract concepts; they must be felt in family homes, children’s classrooms, and young people’s everyday businesses. He called the commemoration an occasion for renewed international solidarity, stronger domestic policies, and active partnerships among governments, civil society, and the private sector, urging participants to forge bold commitments that deliver tangible, lasting progress for every African citizen. Also addressing the session, Deputy High Commissioner Awa Dabo said the story of the right to development cannot be told without Africa. Long before development was firmly established in the global human rights discourse, she noted, African leaders, jurists, and civil society were advancing its essential foundations, including self-determination, sovereignty over natural resources, equitable participation, and international solidarity. “Africa was not simply a beneficiary of the right to development,” she said. “Africa was one of its principal architects.” She pointed to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights as the legally binding expression of this vision, and said Africa’s voice today is not only relevant but indispensable. Forty years on, she warned, formidable barriers remain, among them unequal trading relationships, unsustainable debt, shrinking development finance, and persistent illicit financial flows, with consequences felt most sharply by people already facing poverty, exclusion, and discrimination. Growth achieved at any cost to people and the planet, she stressed, is not development. Describing Agenda 2063 as a powerful roadmap, the Deputy High Commissioner said the task now is implementation: integrating the right to development into national plans, public budgets, monitoring systems, and accountability frameworks. She said the conference’s proposed Addis Ababa Outcome Statement offers a chance to set concrete commitments on domestication, financing, monitoring, and accountability. She added that implementation also depends on international cooperation, noting Africa’s leadership in advancing discussion of a draft international covenant on the right to development. The right, she cautioned, must not be reduced to an adversarial North-South debate, because it is a universal human right relevant to every society and every person. In his opening statement, Ambassador Bankole Adeoye recalled that the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights entered into force six weeks before the UN adopted the Declaration in 1986. Africa, he said, did not wait for the world to proclaim this right, because through Article 22, which recognizes the right of all peoples to economic, social and cultural development, it had already made it binding treaty law. He said the theme captures both Africa’s pride and its impatience, and stressed that resilience must never become the ceiling of its ambition. Ambassador Adeoye said the African Union supports a robust, legally binding International Covenant on the Right to Development. “Declarations inspire, but obligations deliver,” he said. He underscored that Agenda 2063 and its Second Ten-Year Implementation Plan translate Article 22 into measurable outcomes, which must be domesticated in national plans, budgets, and accountability systems. He also noted that in August 2026, the Peace and Security Council requested the integration of human rights indicators into the Continental Early Warning System. On the green transition, the Commissioner said Africa will not accept one that repeats the injustices of past extraction, and called for responsible business conduct, fair financing, debt sustainability, and action against illicit financial flows. He added that artificial intelligence must be governed by equality, participation, transparency, and accountability. Concluding, he said the right to development must be fulfilled “no

ethiopia.title: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests
ethiopia.content: Africa: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests 6 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Political parties must go beyond seeking power and focus on serving citizens, strengthening democratic governance and building consensus on Africa's development priorities, African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf said today. Addressing the second African Political Parties Summit 2026 underway in Addis Ababa, the Chairperson highlighted the central role of political parties in advancing democratic governance, peace and development in line with the African Union Agenda 2063. Youssouf said political parties have three major responsibilities: developing social and economic policies that serve citizens, building bridges between citizens and state institutions, and raising awareness about the broader interests of their countries. "Are they meant to conquer power? Or is the mission wider than that?" he asked, stressing that political parties should serve the public and promote national interests rather than narrow political, ethnic or sectarian interests. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Chairperson also underscored the role of opposition parties in monitoring government actions and ensuring public accountability. On constitutional governance, Youssouf said states have a fundamental responsibility to protect their constitutions, organize credible elections and ensure respect for fundamental freedoms. "In case of disagreements on those critical issues, dialogue must always prevail," he noted. He further highlighted the importance of transparency in political party financing, saying strict rules are necessary to prevent corruption and external influences. Referring to the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, the Chairperson said the instrument recognizes political pluralism and promotes the rights and responsibilities of ruling and opposition parties. He also described the Maputo Protocol as an important foundation for women's participation in political life, emphasizing the need for forums bringing together women and young people to promote greater access to political participation and decision-making. Youssouf stressed that African citizens must be involved in decisions affecting their communities. Turning to Africa's economic future, he described political parties as architects of the continent's future, emphasizing the need for institutions capable of shaping that future around the general public interest rather than partisan considerations. The commitment was made during talks between Ethiopian Defense Minister Mohammed Idris and French Ambassador to Ethiopia Alexis Lamek in Addis Ababa on Wondsday. The meeting, part of the Defense Minister's ongoing military diplomacy engagements with foreign ambassadors, focused on strengthening the two countries' historical ties and expanding cooperation in military and strategic affairs. On the ongoing Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration (DDR) process in the Tigray Region, the Minister urged France to extend the necessary support to ensure its successful implementation. Ambassador Lamek, for his part, reaffirmed France's commitment to strengthening its longstanding relations and multifaceted cooperation with Ethiopia. He underscored his country's readiness to enhance joint efforts in promoting regional peace and stability, while advancing military training and capacity-building cooperation. The renewed commitment signals both countries' interest in translating their longstanding diplomatic relations into stronger practical cooperation in defense, military development and regional security, as ENA learned. ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't 6 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called on African political parties to embrace leadership renewal and build consensus on long-term national priorities. He also stressed that the continent's development must transcend electoral cycles and changes of government. The Prime Minister made the call while opening the Second African Political Parties Summit in Addis Ababa, where he proposed two key commitments for inclusion in the Addis Ababa Declaration: establishing consensus on long-term national development priorities and strengthening leadership development and succession across Africa. He emphasized that political parties should agree on strategic national goals with measurable milestones to ensure continuity of development efforts regardless of political transitions. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines PM Abiy elaborated that parties can maintain ideological and policy differences and compete for electoral support while working together on fundamental national interests and long-term development objectives. He also stressed that leadership succession is essential to sustaining development, warning that countries risk losing hard-won progress when incumbent leaders fail to prepare the next generation of leadership. Highlighting Ethiopia's experience in political inclusiveness, the Prime Minister said the country's reformed government has incorporated leaders from opposition political parties. This reflects an approach that values broader participation and shared responsibility, the Premier revealed. He noted that Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy encourages political actors to recognize and build on one another's contributions despite their differences, particularly when national interests call for collective action. Turning to economic transformation, PM Abiy outlined key measures undertaken through Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda, including opening the telecommunications, banking and competition sectors to foreign participation and introducing a market-based foreign exchange system. He also highlighted the Green Legacy Initiative, noting that more than 50 billion seedlings have been planted since its launch in 2019 through the collective participation of citizens, communities and institutions. The initiative, he explained, is aimed at restoring degraded landscapes, protecting water resources and strengthening national resilience to climate-related challenges, including droughts and floods. somalia.title: Defence Minister Accuses Supreme Court of Foreign Plot, Says Ruling Was an Abu Dhabi Agenda - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Defence Minister Accuses Supreme Court of Foreign Plot, Says Ruling Was an Abu Dhabi Agenda - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Benadir Defence Minister Accuses Supreme Court of Foreign Plot, Says Ruling Was an Abu Dhabi Agenda November 6, 2026 5 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Defence Minister, Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, has escalated his public attack on the Supreme Court and the dismissed Chief Justice, accusing unnamed judges of participating in a foreign-orchestrated plot and claiming the ruling against the government was the product of hired mercenaries and an Abu Dhabi agenda. In a social media post on Friday, Fiqi described the Supreme Court’s ruling as “a legal document that touches reality” but framed it as the failed culmination of a conspiracy organized by foreign actors and executed by “mercenaries” within the judiciary. He claimed that the dismissal of Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed was lawful, and that Baashe’s subsequent flight to the compound of former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed demonstrated that he was executing an agenda “arrived at in the Abu Dhabi meeting.” Fiqi’s statement is the most direct public accusation by a senior federal official that the judiciary was infiltrated by foreign interests. It follows the Supreme Court’s ruling on November 5 that declared the mandates of the President, Parliament, and the Federal Government expired, and ordered elections within 90 days, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the ruling . The court had also declared Baashe’s dismissal “null and void,” a decision the Attorney General has rejected as lacking legal basis. The Abu Dhabi Allegation The Defence Minister’s reference to the “Abu Dhabi meeting” echoes a claim that has circulated in Somali political circles for months. In October, NISA Director Mahad Mohamed Salad alleged that opposition figures, including Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Abdirahman Abdishakur Warsame, had met in the UAE to discuss forming an armed rebellion against the government, as FTL Somalia reported on the NISA chief’s allegations . The government has not publicly presented evidence to substantiate the claim, and the opposition has denied it. The Supreme Court’s ruling, which was issued in response to a petition filed by Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, is now being framed by the government as the product of that alleged conspiracy. Fiqi’s statement is an attempt to delegitimize the ruling by tying it to a foreign plot and to the opposition figure who brought the case. The accusation also targets Sharif directly. Fiqi asked how Sharif could be accepted as a legitimate actor when he claims to have been attacked while offering his home as a refuge to “anyone who harms statehood and works for foreign interests.” The statement positions the former President as the protector of a judge the government considers a fugitive, and by extension, as complicit in the alleged foreign agenda. A Government on the Defensive Fiqi’s intervention is a sign that the government is not prepared to accept the court’s ruling or de-escalate. The Attorney General has already rejected the ruling as lacking legal basis, and troops were deployed around the Supreme Court and to the Chief Justice’s residence, as the opposition accused the President of deploying troops to arrest Baashe . The strategy appears to be threefold: deny the legitimacy of the ruling, discredit the judges who issued it, and frame the opposition as agents of foreign powers. Whether that strategy will succeed depends on whether the public and international partners accept the government’s narrative. The court’s ruling is detailed and grounded in constitutional text. Fiqi’s accusation is a political claim without publicly presented evidence. The government is asking the public to believe that the judiciary was infiltrated, without showing how, when, or by whom. Critical Note Ahmed Moallim Fiqi’s statement is not a legal argument. It is a political attack dressed in the language of national security. He accuses unnamed judges of being foreign mercenaries, claims the ruling was orchestrated from Abu Dhabi, and describes the Chief Justice as a fugitive who fled to Sharif Sheikh Ahmed’s compound. These are serious allegations. They are also unsubstantiated. The government has a right to challenge the court’s ruling. The Attorney General has filed objections, and the government can pursue legal remedies. But the Defence Minister’s statement does not pursue legal remedies. It pursues a narrative. It tells the public that the court is corrupt, that the opposition is foreign-funded, and that the government is the only defender of Somali sovereignty. That narrative may be effective in the short term. It is corrosive in the long term. The deeper problem is that the government’s accusations cut both ways. If the judiciary can be infiltrated by foreign interests, so can the executive. If a judge can be a mercenary, so can a minister. The government has not explained why its own claims about the Abu Dhabi plot should be believed without evidence, while the court’s detailed constitutional reasoning should be dismissed as a foreign conspiracy. The public is being asked to choose between two narratives, neither of which has been independently verified. The Supreme Court’s ruling has declared the President’s mandate expired. The government is rejecting that ruling and attacking the judges who issued it. Fiqi’s statement is the clearest sign yet that the government will not comply. It will fight. The question is what it will fight with, and whether the institutions it is attacking will survive the assault. somalia.title: Somalia’s WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Somalia's WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Economy & Business Nationwide Somalia’s WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu November 6, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s decade-long bid to join the World Trade Organization has moved closer to completion after a week-long technical mission in Mogadishu brought most of its accession documents close to final, ahead of a working party meeting expected in 2027. A team led by the WTO’s Head of Accessions Division, working alongside experts from the International Trade Centre at the Somali government’s request, spent October 10 to 15 reviewing the documents behind Somalia’s bid. The mission, funded by the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office through the ITC’s Making Trade Happen project, refined Somalia’s replies to WTO members’ questions on customs, import licensing, animal and plant health, technical standards, and intellectual property, and mapped the laws still needed for compliance . The teams also prepared Somalia’s first offers to open its markets for goods and services. A joint session with the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area examined how Somalia’s regional commitments and its WTO bid can reinforce each other. Somalia joined the EAC in 2024, and the bloc’s common external tariff will shape its offer on goods . “The UK is proud to support Somalia’s ambition to join the World Trade Organization through our partnership with the International Trade Centre. Bringing WTO expertise to Mogadishu for the first time is helping turn that ambition into practical progress,” said British Ambassador to Somalia Charles King . “Ultimately, this is about creating opportunities for businesses, attracting investment and creating jobs for Somalis.” The Economic Case Somalia applied to join the WTO in 2015, and its working party first met in Geneva in February 2025. Somali leaders have framed accession as a route to growth and investment, arguing that binding international rules on trade would reduce the uncertainty that deters foreign investors and open markets for Somali products . The economic logic is straightforward, though the starting point is difficult. Somalia has about 18 million people and the longest coastline on the African mainland, but its exports remain concentrated in livestock. Live animal sales earned $576 million in 2025, mostly in the Gulf, according to ITC Trade Map, more than double the export earnings from seven years ago . As FTL Somalia reported on the concentration of Somalia’s export base , livestock still accounts for roughly 75 percent of exports, leaving the economy vulnerable to import bans and price shocks in a single sector. WTO membership could help address that vulnerability. The organization’s rules on animal health and food safety provide a framework that importing countries recognize, potentially clearing a path for Somali livestock exports to markets that currently restrict them. But the path is not automatic. Somalia would need to demonstrate that its veterinary controls, inspection systems, and certification procedures meet international standards, and it would need to maintain those standards consistently. The broader trade picture is also challenging. As FTL Somalia reported on Somalia’s trade gap , imports continue to far outstrip exports, creating a structural deficit that WTO membership alone cannot resolve. Joining the organization would lower barriers to Somali goods in foreign markets, but it would also require Somalia to lower its own barriers, exposing domestic producers to competition they may not be ready to face. Regional Integration and the WTO Track Somalia’s WTO bid is not proceeding in isolation. The country joined the EAC in 2024 and formally acceded to the African Continental Free Trade Area as its 50th member, opening access to a market of 1.4 billion consumers, as FTL Somalia reported on the AfCFTA accession . The two tracks are complementary in principle. The EAC’s common external tariff will shape Somalia’s WTO offer on goods, and the AfCFTA provides a framework for expanding intra-African trade that the WTO’s global rules do not directly address. But they also create complexity. Somalia’s negotiators must ensure that its commitments to the EAC and the AfCFTA are consistent with its WTO obligations, and that the preferences it grants to regional partners do not violate the WTO’s most-favored-nation principle. The government has framed regional integration as a means of creating opportunities for Somali traders, as FTL Somalia reported on the minister’s remarks about EAC membership . The WTO accession process adds a global dimension to that strategy, but it also imposes disciplines that the government will need to implement across customs, standards, and regulatory agencies that are still being built. Critical Note The WTO mission to Mogadishu is a genuine step forward. The fact that WTO and ITC experts spent a week working alongside Somali officials, refining documents and preparing market access offers, is evidence that the accession process has moved beyond rhetoric into technical work. The UK’s funding and the ITC’s expertise have made that work possible. But the completion of accession documents is not the same as accession. Somalia still needs to finalize its offers, answer remaining questions from WTO members, enact the laws it has mapped, and demonstrate that it can implement the commitments it makes. The working party meeting expected in 2027 is a milestone, not a finish line. Accession negotiations can take years, and the terms Somalia accepts will determine whether membership delivers the benefits its leaders promise. The economic case is real but conditional. WTO rules can help Somali livestock reach new markets, but only if Somalia can meet the health and safety standards those rules require. Membership can attract investment, but only if the legal and regulatory environment is stable enough to reassure investors. And it can support regional integration, but only if Somalia’s commitments to the EAC, the AfCFTA, and the WTO are coherent and consistently implemented. The government has spent a decade pursuing WTO membership. The technical mission in October brought that goal closer. The harder work, of building the institutions and implementing the rules that membership requires, is still ahead. The documents are nearly final. The capacity to honor them is not. somalia.title: Attorney General Rejects Supreme Court Ruling as "Lacking Legal Basis" in Deepening Constitutional Standoff - Somali News today Live - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Attorney General Rejects Supreme Court Ruling as "Lacking Legal Basis" in Deepening Constitutional Standoff - Somali News today Live MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Attorney General has formally rejected the Supreme Court’s ruling on the constitutional case and the Chief Justice’s dismissal, declaring the court’s decision “lacking any legal basis” and vowing to take “appropriate legal action,” in a move that deepens the constitutional standoff between the executive and the judiciary. In a statement issued on November 6, the Office of the Attorney General said it had submitted legal objections to the Supreme Court regarding the court’s jurisdiction and the legal standing of the petitioner, former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed. It accused the judges of violating procedural rules, failing to respond to its objections, and “creating a new case” that was not the one originally filed. As FTL Somalia reported when the Attorney General first demanded amendment records , the government had been preparing its legal defense since October, requesting documentation from both houses of parliament and the Justice Ministry ahead of its scheduled response to the court. The Attorney General’s intervention came a day after the Supreme Court issued a sweeping ruling that declared the mandates of the President, Parliament, and the Federal Government expired in 2026, and ordered elections within 90 days. The court had also declared President Mohamud’s dismissal of Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed “null and void” and accused the presidency of attempting to obstruct the constitutional case, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the constitutional standoff . The Attorney General’s Objections The Attorney General’s statement laid out a series of procedural complaints against the court. It argued that the court should have first ruled on the government’s legal objections before issuing a judgment, and that it violated the principle of adversarial proceedings by not allowing both sides to be heard. It further accused the court of violating its own structural rules, alleging that the Chief Justice should have presided over the panel of judges hearing the case, and that the court “created a new case” by ruling on matters that were not part of the original petition. The statement concluded that the court’s ruling “does not serve the national interest or the completion of the building of the Somali state” and therefore “has no legal effect.” The Attorney General’s Office said it would “take the appropriate legal step.” A Standoff With No Clear Resolution The Attorney General’s rejection of the ruling marks the latest escalation in a confrontation that has moved from the courtroom to the streets. On Thursday, Somali government troops deployed in large numbers around the Supreme Court, and Chief Justice Baashe was ordered to leave the premises, according to a senior judge who spoke to BBC Somali. The court’s official Facebook page, which had been used to publish recent rulings, was also taken offline. The allegation was first raised publicly by opposition presidential candidate Abdirahman Abdishakur Warsame, who accused the President of deploying troops to arrest the Chief Justice, as FTL Somalia reported on the opposition accusation . Former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire also accused the President of launching “an assault on the Supreme Court” and deploying troops to its premises, claiming that the Chief Justice and lawyers were “being pursued in their homes for arrest” and that the court’s operations had been halted. His claims could not be independently verified, but images published by Somali media claimed to show military forces in the court’s compound. The presidency has not publicly responded to the Supreme Court’s term-limit ruling, the court’s rejection of the Chief Justice’s dismissal, or the allegations of troop deployment. The Political and Security Context The crisis unfolds against a backdrop of multiple pressures. The United Nations political mission closed a week before the ruling, leaving no agreed mediator for the election dispute. Uganda, the largest contributor to the African Union force, has announced it will withdraw all troops by the end of 2027, and Washington has cut funding for the UN logistics mission that supports the coalition. The opposition has unified behind the court’s ruling. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who brought the challenge, welcomed the judgment and urged the president to negotiate. Former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo had already warned that proceeding without consensus would trigger parallel elections and renewed conflict , and had accused Mohamud of sabotaging internationally mediated talks . As the unravelling of Somalia’s security architecture continues, a political crisis without a clear mechanism for resolution is exactly what analysts warned against. Adnan Abdi Ali, a political analyst at the Somali Center for Studies in Mogadishu, questioned whether the ruling would be enforced at all. “This ruling is unlikely to be implemented, as it comes at a time of ongoing electoral disputes,” he said. Critical Note The Attorney General’s statement is not a legal argument. It is a political declaration dressed in legal language. It accuses the court of procedural violations, but it does not engage with the substance of the ruling: that the President’s mandate expired in May 2026, that the constitutional amendments cannot be applied retroactively to sitting institutions, and that the Chief Justice’s dismissal violated the constitution. The government’s response to the ruling has been consistent: deny its legitimacy, reject its authority, and refuse to engage with its findings. The Attorney General’s office says the ruling “has no legal effect.” But a ruling does not cease to have legal effect because the government says so. It ceases to have effect when a higher authority overturns it, or when the institutions it binds choose to ignore it. There is no higher authority in Somalia’s judicial system than the Supreme Court. The only question now is whether the government will obey the ruling or defy it. The troop deployment around the court, the removal of its Facebook page, and the Attorney General’s rejection of its ruling all point in the same direction. The government is not preparing to comply. It is preparing to govern as if the ruling does not exist. That is a choice with consequences. It means the judiciary has been effectively neutralized as a check on executive power. It means the opposition has no legal venue left to challenge the government’s authority. And it means that the political crisis will not be resolved through law. It will be resolved through whatever means the two sides can bring to bear, and the country will be the poorer for it. somalia.summary: Somalia's Attorney General has rejected a Supreme Court ruling regarding a constitutional case, labeling it as "lacking any legal basis." This rejection escalates the ongoing standoff between the executive and judiciary branches. In a statement on November 6, the Attorney General criticized the court for procedural violations, claiming it failed to address legal objections raised by the government and improperly ruled on issues not included in the original petition. The Supreme Court had previously declared the mandates of the President and Parliament expired in 2026 and ordered elections within 90 days. Following the ruling, government troops were deployed around the Supreme Court, raising concerns about the safety of the Chief Justice and court operations. The political crisis is compounded by the withdrawal of international support and a lack of mediation for the electoral dispute. Analysts suggest that the ruling may not be enforced, indicating a troubling trend of diminishing judicial authority in Somalia.

somalia.title: Former Spy Chief Sanbaloolshe Returns to Beledweyne with Armed Convoy, Backing Breakaway Hiiraan Administration - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Former Spy Chief Sanbaloolshe Returns to Beledweyne with Armed Convoy, Backing Breakaway Hiiraan Administration - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Hirshabelle Former Spy Chief Sanbaloolshe Returns to Beledweyne with Armed Convoy, Backing Breakaway Hiiraan Administration November 6, 2026 7 min read BELEDWEYNE , Somalia’s former intelligence chief, Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbaloolshe, has returned to Beledweyne, arriving with a military convoy amid a deepening political dispute over the leadership of Hirshabelle and growing calls for Hiiraan to establish an administration independent of the regional government. Sanbaloolshe’s arrival was confirmed by multiple sources, with local community fighters having recently occupied regional administration offices in the city. The former NISA director has backed calls for a separate administration in Hiiraan, a position that places him at the center of a confrontation with the Hirshabelle administration and, by extension, the federal government in Mogadishu. The return is not a routine political visit. Reports indicate that Sanbaloolshe crossed from Ethiopia with a significant armed convoy, with some sources citing as many as 28 Land Cruisers and a large number of armed men. The movement of personnel and vehicles from Ethiopian territory has raised questions about external involvement in a dispute that is increasingly taking on the dimensions of an armed challenge to federal authority. A Dispute Rooted in Representation and Power The immediate context for Sanbaloolshe’s return is the disputed leadership of Hirshabelle. Ali Gudlawe was re-elected president of the regional state in Jowhar on October 24, a vote that Hiiraan’s political leaders and traditional elders rejected, arguing that no leadership should be chosen without an inclusive political agreement addressing the region’s representation. The Hawadle clan, dominant in Hiiraan, has long argued that the presidency of Hirshabelle should rotate to their community under the original power-sharing arrangement that established the state in 2016. Gudlawe’s re-election, and the appointment of a new Hiiraan governor loyal to him, deepened that grievance. As local Macawiisley fighters mobilised in Beledweyne ahead of the vote, they seized voter registration centers and disrupted the electoral process. Sanbaloolshe, a Hawadle figure with deep roots in Hiiraan, has positioned himself as the political leader of this movement. In an interview that circulated in late October, he said he and his supporters were building a new administration for Hiiraan, and he did not rule out cooperation with Al-Shabaab when asked directly. He also claimed to have met the leaders of Puntland, Jubaland, and Somaliland in the UAE to seek support for an armed rebellion in Hiiraan, and said the movement would seek Ethiopian backing. None of those leaders commented, and he offered no evidence for the claim. The External Dimension The allegation of Ethiopian involvement is not new. Sanbaloolshe has long been regarded in Somali political circles as one of Addis Ababa’s most trusted interlocutors, a perception reinforced by his reported entry from Ethiopian territory with an armed convoy. Reports in late October claimed he had requested young men from Beledweyne to travel to Ethiopia to collect military vehicles allegedly provided to him, though the purpose and official status of that support remain unconfirmed. The UAE is also a factor. Sanbaloolshe’s relationships with both Addis Ababa and Abu Dhabi are described as historical, built through years of intelligence cooperation and political patronage. When the federal government severed its agreements with the UAE in January 2026, it was Sanbaloolshe, an MP without a formal portfolio, who was reportedly dispatched to Abu Dhabi to manage the fallout. That episode underscores his utility as a back-channel operator, and it explains why his return to Hiiraan is being watched closely by Mogadishu. Confidential sources cited by Red Sea Axis have gone further, alleging that the campaign to which Sanbaloolshe is attached is financed by the UAE, supported by Israeli intelligence, and carried out through Kenyan intermediaries, with the aim of confining the federal government’s authority to Mogadishu. These are serious allegations that have not been independently verified, but they align with the broader pattern of external engagement in Somalia’s federal disputes that has been documented in the government’s accusations against Abu Dhabi . The Federal Response Villa Somalia has been meeting to address the crisis. According to reports, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud convened a high-level meeting with MPs and the deputy commander of the Hirshabelle forces to discuss how to counter the Hiiraan movement, regain control of the Lamagalaay camp, and weaken clan unity through financial incentives and political engagement. The meeting reflects the federal government’s recognition that the situation in Beledweyne is not a peripheral dispute but a direct challenge to its authority in central Somalia. The federal government’s dilemma is acute. Sanbaloolshe is a figure it cannot easily dismiss. He has served as NISA director three times, including under President Mohamud, and his network extends into the intelligence services, clan structures, and foreign capitals that matter to Mogadishu. As Hiiraan Online noted in a profile of Sanbaloolshe, “the man you cannot kill, you must feed.” That logic explains why Mohamud has kept Sanbaloolshe close in the past, and why his current move is so destabilizing. The security context makes the standoff more dangerous. About two thousand Macawiisley fighters have left the frontlines against Al-Shabaab and returned to Beledweyne, weakening the campaign against the militants in Hiiraan while strengthening the forces available to the Hiiraan administration movement. As the governance vacuum fuels clan mobilisation in other regions when security presence recedes, the withdrawal of fighters from the frontlines creates an opening that Al-Shabaab is likely to exploit. Critical Note Sanbaloolshe’s return to Beledweyne is the most serious challenge to federal authority in central Somalia since the Laftagareen standoff in South West State. It is not a spontaneous uprising. It is a calculated political and military move by a former intelligence chief who knows the system from the inside, who has cultivated relationships with the external actors whose support matters, and who has positioned himself as the champion of a genuine grievance: the marginalisation of Hiiraan within a Hirshabelle state that was designed to share power but has instead concentrated it in Jowhar. The federal government’s response has so far been reactive. It has met, it has discussed financial incentives and political engagement, and it has considered how to retake a military camp. These are the tools of a government that is managing a crisis, not resolving one. The underlying grievance, the Hawadle demand for a fair share of power in Hirshabelle, will not be addressed by buying off MPs or retaking a compound. It requires a political settlement that the current Hirshabelle leadership has shown no willingness to accept. The external dimension is the wild card. If Sanbaloolshe is indeed receiving support from Ethiopia, the UAE, or both, then the federal government is not simply facing a domestic insurgency. It is facing a proxy challenge from actors who have their own reasons for weakening Mogadishu’s authority. The federal government’s own relationships with those actors are complex, and its ability to counter their influence is limited. What happens in Beledweyne in the coming days will determine whether Hiiraan becomes a third front in Somalia’s fragmenting federal project, alongside Puntland and Jubaland, or whether the dispute can be contained through negotiation. As the unravelling of Somalia’s security architecture continues and the federal government’s political capital is consumed by one crisis after another, the Macawiisley fighters are in the city, the former spy chief is among them, and Mogadishu faces another confrontation it cannot afford to lose. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, File) SS JVR Make us a preferred source on Google flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar : By Omar Faruk The Associated Press MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Somalia’s power struggle has deepened after the Supreme Court ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term had expired and ordered elections within 90 days. The court’s decision on Thursday came a day after Mohamud dismissed the country’s chief justice. The presidency had not responded to the ruling by Friday. The confrontation comes a week after the United Nations closed its political mission , which had helped rival leaders negotiate. No replacement mediator has been agreed upon for an election dispute that has already sparked armed clashes in the capital, Mogadishu. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Court rejects another year in power The Supreme Court’s five-page judgment, reviewed by The Associated Press, rejected the president’s position that constitutional changes allow him to remain in office until 2027. The court said parliament’s decision to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years did not give current officeholders another year in power. It ruled that their terms had already expired. Judges gave political leaders 30 days to agree on how to hold elections and limited the government to routine administration pending a vote. They did not name a replacement president or specify what would happen if the deadlines were missed. In announcing Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed’s dismissal, the presidency cited complaints about the administration of justice and the need for judicial reform. The Supreme Court rejected his removal, saying the president had violated the constitution and accusing him of trying to obstruct its review of the term extensions. Local news outlet Hiiraan Online reported Friday that government troops had deployed around the Supreme Court on Thursday and that the chief justice had been ordered to leave. The AP could not independently verify the report. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who brought the challenge, welcomed the judgment and urged the president to negotiate. Adnan Abdi Ali, a political analyst at the Somali Center for Studies in Mogadishu, questioned whether the ruling would be enforced. “This ruling is unlikely to be implemented, as it comes at a time of ongoing electoral disputes,” he said. The dispute also concerns how Somalis will vote. The president wants direct elections to replace a system in which clan representatives choose lawmakers, who then elect the president. Opposition leaders and the regional governments of Puntland and Jubaland have challenged his constitutional and electoral changes. Troop withdrawal adds security uncertainty Ugandan troops had been deployed under a bilateral agreement with Somalia that helped recapture and hold territory against al-Qaida-linked al-Shabab militants. African Union peacekeepers plan to replace them at four bases critical to protecting Mogadishu, but it remains unclear who will secure the positions those peacekeepers leave behind. Uganda says its remaining forces, including AU peacekeepers, will leave by the end of 2027. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Al-Shabab still controls large rural areas and attacks Mogadishu and other cities. Ahead of the U.N. political mission’s closure, Mohamed Husein Gaas, director of the Mogadishu-based RAAD Peace Research Institute, warned that competing claims to power could undermine cooperation among security forces. “Somalia could find itself confronting a political crisis without an agreed mechanism to contain it,” he told the AP. ___ Associated Press writer Khaled Kazziha in Nairobi, Kenya, contributed to this report. This decision intensifies the ongoing power struggle in the country, particularly following Mohamud's dismissal of the chief justice just a day prior. The court rejected the president's claim that constitutional amendments allowed him to remain in office until 2027, stating that the parliamentary decision to extend terms did not apply retroactively. Political leaders have been given 30 days to agree on election procedures, while the government is restricted to routine administration. The ruling comes amid heightened tensions, with armed clashes reported in Mogadishu and the recent closure of the UN political mission, which had facilitated negotiations among rival factions. Analysts express skepticism about the ruling's enforcement, given the existing electoral disputes and the challenges posed by the al-Shabab militant group.

The Somali delegation was led by the Minister of Commerce and Industry, H.E. Jamal Mohamed Hassan. During the exhibition, representatives of Somalia’s economic ministries showcased the country’s products, natural resources and investment opportunities to international participants. Somalia’s participation placed particular emphasis on the country’s mineral resources, highlighting the diverse deposits found across its territory, including metallic minerals, gemstones, decorative stones and other valuable mineral resources. The exhibition provided an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate the potential of its natural resources while attracting the attention of international investors to opportunities in the country’s growing economic sectors. Somalia’s participation also forms part of the Federal Government’s broader efforts to strengthen international trade relations, encourage foreign direct investment and promote domestic production. Through its presence at the exhibition, Somalia reaffirmed its commitment to expanding economic cooperation with international partners and positioning the country as an emerging destination for trade and investment. Farah Abdi Warsameh - AP Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Somalia’s power struggle has deepened after the Supreme Court ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term had expired and ordered elections within 90 days. The court's decision on Thursday came a day after Mohamud dismissed the country's chief justice. The presidency had not responded to the ruling by Friday. The confrontation comes a week after the United Nations closed its political mission , which had helped rival leaders negotiate. No replacement mediator has been agreed upon for an election dispute that has already sparked armed clashes in the capital, Mogadishu. Court rejects another year in power The Supreme Court's five-page judgment, reviewed by The Associated Press, rejected the president’s position that constitutional changes allow him to remain in office until 2027. The court said parliament’s decision to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years did not give current officeholders another year in power. It ruled that their terms had already expired. Judges gave political leaders 30 days to agree on how to hold elections and limited the government to routine administration pending a vote. They did not name a replacement president or specify what would happen if the deadlines were missed. In announcing Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed’s dismissal, the presidency cited complaints about the administration of justice and the need for judicial reform. The Supreme Court rejected his removal, saying the president had violated the constitution and accusing him of trying to obstruct its review of the term extensions. Local news outlet Hiiraan Online reported Friday that government troops had deployed around the Supreme Court on Thursday and that the chief justice had been ordered to leave. The AP could not independently verify the report. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who brought the challenge, welcomed the judgment and urged the president to negotiate. Adnan Abdi Ali, a political analyst at the Somali Center for Studies in Mogadishu, questioned whether the ruling would be enforced. “This ruling is unlikely to be implemented, as it comes at a time of ongoing electoral disputes,” he said. The dispute also concerns how Somalis will vote. The president wants direct elections to replace a system in which clan representatives choose lawmakers, who then elect the president. Opposition leaders and the regional governments of Puntland and Jubaland have challenged his constitutional and electoral changes. Troop withdrawal adds security uncertainty Ugandan troops had been deployed under a bilateral agreement with Somalia that helped recapture and hold territory against al-Qaida-linked al-Shabab militants. African Union peacekeepers plan to replace them at four bases critical to protecting Mogadishu, but it remains unclear who will secure the positions those peacekeepers leave behind. Uganda says its remaining forces, including AU peacekeepers, will leave by the end of 2027. Al-Shabab still controls large rural areas and attacks Mogadishu and other cities. Ahead of the U.N. political mission’s closure, Mohamed Husein Gaas, director of the Mogadishu-based RAAD Peace Research Institute, warned that competing claims to power could undermine cooperation among security forces. “Somalia could find itself confronting a political crisis without an agreed mechanism to contain it,” he told the AP. Associated Press writer Khaled Kazziha in Nairobi, Kenya, contributed to this report. somalia.summary: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension is unlawful, declaring that his term has expired and mandating elections within 90 days. This decision intensifies the ongoing power struggle in the country, which has faced political instability and challenges in governance. The ruling comes amid a backdrop of heightened tensions and concerns over the electoral process, as the nation grapples with security issues, including threats from the militant group Al-Shabaab. The court's order for immediate elections aims to restore democratic processes, but it also raises questions about the potential for further conflict among political factions. As the situation unfolds, the international community is closely monitoring developments in Somalia, hoping for a peaceful resolution that can lead to stability and effective governance in the region.

football.title: الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ - winwin
football.content: الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ من مباراة الهلال ضد رايون سبورت الرواندي (Facebook/alhilalsc.official) 5 نوفمبر 2026 الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أحبط الهلال جماهيره وانقاد للتعادل بنتيجة 1-1 أمام نظيره رايون سبورت الرواندي، اليوم الأربعاء 4 نوفمبر، على ملعب "كيغالي بيليه" ضمن الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي، الذي يشهد مشاركة الهلال ومواطنه المريخ . وفرط "الموج الأزرق" في فرصة تحقيق الفوز، مكتفيا بالتعادل بعد أن بادر بالتسجيل عبر قائده وهدافه محمد عبد الرحمن، قبل أن يدرك المنافس التعادل في الرمق الأخير من المباراة، ليهدر الفريق فرصة مثالية لتقليص الفارق مع صدارة الدوري، في انتظار خوض مبارياته المؤجلة الثلاث. مكاسب مضاعفة لـ"غربال" رغم تفريط الهلال في الفوز باستقباله هدف التعادل في اللحظات الأخيرة، إلا أن "الكابيتانو" محمد عبد الرحمن نجح في وضع فريقه بالمقدمة بهدف رائع، محققا مكاسب شخصية بتعزيز سجله التهديفي وتأكيد عودته القوية قبل المواجهات المرتقبة في مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا عقب فترة التوقف الدولي. كما سيمنح مدرب المنتخب "كواسي أبياه" خياراً هجومياً مميزاً لاستعادة فاعلية "صقور الجديان" التهديفية، بخوضه مباراتين حاسمتين أمام المنتخب السنغالي بتصفيات بطولة الأمم الأفريقية. اقرأ أيضًا مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري وسيحظى مدرب النادي الأزرق بفرصة مثالية لتجهيز عناصره عبر خوض تجارب ودية قوية خلال فترة التوقف الدولي، إذ سيلتحق 16 من أبرز نجومه بمنتخباتهم الوطنية، منهم 13 لاعبا في صفوف "صقور الجديان", و3 آخرون مع منتخبات بلدانهم. وسيعمل المدرب خلال هذا الغياب على إعداد البدائل، سعيا لتحقيق أفضل النتائج في دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا. وقرر المدرب جوزيف زينباور استغلال فترة التوقف بإجراء مباريات إعدادية، على أن يخوض الفريق مواجهة واحدة في الدوري الرواندي عقب التوقف، ليبدأ بعدها رحلة شاقة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بملاقاة حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر الجاري، ثم يحل ضيفا على المغرب الفاسي في 5 ديسمبر المقبل، قبل أن يختتم هذه المرحلة الأولى بصدام قوي أمام بيراميدز المصري. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق football.summary: تعادل فريق الهلال السوداني مع رايون سبورت الرواندي بنتيجة 1-1 في مباراة أقيمت يوم 4 نوفمبر 2026، ضمن الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي. رغم البداية القوية بتسجيل قائد الفريق محمد عبد الرحمن هدف التقدم، إلا أن الهلال أهدر فرصة الفوز بعد أن أدرك المنافس التعادل في اللحظات الأخيرة. هذا التعادل أحبط جماهير الهلال، لكنه يحمل بعض المكاسب، حيث عزز عبد الرحمن سجله التهديفي، مما يعزز فرصه في المباريات المقبلة، خاصة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. المدرب جوزيف زينباور يخطط لاستغلال فترة التوقف الدولي لإجراء مباريات ودية، حيث سيلتحق 16 لاعباً من الهلال بمنتخباتهم الوطنية. بعد فترة التوقف، سيواجه الهلال حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر، ثم المغرب الفاسي وبيراميدز المصري، مما يتطلب تجهيز الفريق بشكل جيد لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية.

فترة الانتقالات الصيفية، مشيرًا إلى أن فترة التوقف الدولي ستساعده في تجهيز الفريق بشكل أفضل. مدرب الهلال يشيد بنجميه كما أشاد زينباور بنجميه سفيان فريد و مصطفى كرشوم ، قائلا: "قدم الحارس سفيان مباراة متميزة، ويعد كرشوم مدافعا رائعا يمتاز بالهدوء والقدرة الفائقة على استخلاص الكرة وبناء اللعب". وأضاف: "تقدمنا مبكرا ولم نستثمر الفرص التي أتيحت لنا، واستقبلنا هدفا في الرمق الأخير من المباراة؛ كان يتعين علينا تسجيل هدفين على الأقل لنحسم المباراة، ولكننا لم نستثمر الفرص، علينا إيجاد حلول لاستقبال الأهداف المتأخرة، وبالمجمل، لست راضيا عن هذه النتيجة". اقرأ أيضًا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا كما كشف زينباور عن أسباب تذبذب الأداء والتغييرات المستمرة في تشكيل فريقه مؤخرًا، قائلا: "لقد أضفنا عناصر جديدة خلال فترة الانتقالات، لدينا لاعبون شباب نرغب في منحهم فرصة المشاركة؛ لذا نجري هذه التعديلات لنقف على مستوياتهم، ونأمل أن يقدموا الإضافة المرجوة". وأضاف: "واجهنا منافسين أقوياء، على غرار فريق رايون الذي تميز باللياقة العالية والقوة البدنية، وسنواجه تحديات صعبة تستدعي وفرة في العناصر". وختم المدرب الألماني حديثه قائلاً: "نسعى لمزيد من التطور، ويتعين علينا مواصلة العمل الجاد لاستثمار الفرص في تطوير الجوانب البدنية والتكتيكية قبل المباريات الصعبة التي تنتظرنا في دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، إذ يجب أن نستعد جيدا لنبلغ مرحلة متميزة من الجاهزية حتى نتمكن من مجابهة التحديات المرتقبة". النشرة البريدية اشترك
